The project is seeking to create an online portal to host information about the TE2100 10 year plan. Feedback from users of the [current Thames Estuary 2100 Plan|https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/322061/LIT7540_43858f.pdf] show that the Plan is difficult to access, and use with bulky hard-copy or pdf documents. This has resulted in users finding it hard to located information. Also the Plan is based on geographical location but finding the information by location is difficult without a geographical search element. 

The update to the Plan, 10 years on from its development, provides an opportunity to provide a more accessible platform for the Plan and make it easier for stakeholders to find what they need and use. An online platform for the updated Thames Estuary 2100 Plan is being sought that will: • be searchable • have data set out geographically • keeps all the accessible from one location • can be easily updated at regular intervals (ideally with direct access for the internal team to do this without having to use an external third party) • is secure • can be branded with the Thames Estuary 2100 branding and partner logos (this is another key outcome of the current 10-Year review project) • can be delivered using Agile project management or similar where users can be involved in development • potentially has different levels of access/areas for different stakeholders • has the ability to hold downloadable pdf guidance documents in a library or similar This project is very similar to an in-delivery project called the National Strategy Portal which is currently in discovery.

There are thousands of man-made and natural obstacles in the rivers of the UK. Many of the man-made obstacles perform important functions - for example dams, sluices, weirs and road culverts - but they can also cause problems such as restricting the movement of fish, damaging river banks and beds, and posing a hazard to people using boats, canoes and kayaks.

We know where many of these obstacles are and what kind of impacts they cause, but we suspect that there are many more obstacles that we don’t know about, particularly in the more remote, upland areas of the UK. For this reason the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (SEPA), the Rivers and Fisheries Trust for Scotland (RAFTS) and the Environment Agency (EA) have joined forces to create this free to use mobile app for iPhone and Android devices that will enable people to send in photos and details of obstacles that they see when they’re out and about either on, in or by the UK’s rivers.

The information received from this app will be used by public bodies, groups of river users, local authorities and private companies to identify redundant man made obstacles that can be removed from rivers, and prioritise improvements to other obstacles that will yield the biggest environmental improvements. Information on natural obstacles will also be used to determine the natural limits to movement for different species of fish.

Provides the functionality for the main user journey. Members of the public or flood risk specialists can use the Flood Map for Planning (FMFP) system to find out which flood zone a proposed building site is in.

Users enter a location (postcode, national grid reference or easting and northing) and are presented with a map of their area of interest. One they have confirmed their location, they will be given information about their probability of flooding. If their location is in a flood zone, the user is informed that they need to carry out a flood risk assessment for any planning activities. They are also advised to check the Environment Agency’s standing advice. Links are provided to supporting information.

+User Stories+

User stories should be simple, unambiguous and independent of all other stories in the project. Initially a story is a high-level definition of a requirement, which is expanded in detail the closer it comes to being developed

The format of a story should be as follows:

*_As a ……….._*
*_I want ………_*
*_So that ………_*



+Acceptance Criteria+

A core aspect of a story is the acceptance criteria, which covers what both the Product Owner (PO) and Quality Analyst (QA) expect from the delivery team in order for it to be signed off as done. The acceptance criteria is the foundation of acceptance testing.

Acceptance criteria will be written at the same time as the user story, and will be written as Gherkin scenarios. These scenarios will be the basis of automated acceptance tests:

*_Scenario: …_*
*_Given ……_*
*_And…._*
*_When ……_*
*_Then ……_*
*_And ......._*

h1. *Backlog Refinement and Sprint Planning*

+Backlog Refinement+

The process will involve the Product owner(PO), Business Analyst(BA), Dev and QA to discuss and refine stories so that all parties have the same understanding of what the story is about. QA will bring an abstract view of the service, defining valid and invalid scenarios in an effort to prevent issues and defects. Stories should have a full set of acceptance criteria and QA should have an in-depth understanding of the stories by the end of the session.

h1. *Types of testing*

The following details the types of testing used in delivery of the service.

* +*Unit Testing*+

All unit testing is automated, and integrated into the Jenkins (CI) build and deployment process. Should a test fail the build will also fail. We write unit tests as part of delivering a story.

* +*Acceptance & automated testing*+

Acceptance testing is based on acceptance criteria outlined in each user story for the project. Testing should cover the complete service for all journeys. When a journey has been signed off it should be added to an automated test suite to be run as part of the continuous integration process for new development builds.

* +*Exploratory testing*+

As part of ‘ways of working’, all completed stories and bugs have to undergo exploratory testing before they are then passed to the product owner for sign off. This work is done by the QA representative on the team as part of sign off for a story.

* +*Browser testing*+

The service is required to be compliant with a number of browsers on different operating systems (OS), and that it is at least functional on some older ones.

* +*Device testing*+

The service is also required to be compliant across a number of devices. As it is a manual process, we don’t test every possible device but instead cycle through them as part of the QA sign off for a story.

* +*Accessibility testing*+

To be GDS compliant the service needs usable by as many people as possible, including those with disabilities. GDS dictates that the WCAG 2.0 standard is used as accessibility guidelines

* +*Performance testing*+

Performance testing is used to help us understand how the service performs under various loads, and confirms that it remains stable during anticipated, peak and exceptional usage.

*Continuous integration*

* After a code commit in Github, the change is built and tested immediately in Jenkins against a feature branch.
* Each commit code is built and tested in isolation. 
* If testing passes, the commit is pushed to candidate branch with other scheduled release changes ready to be tested against the automated test scripts in Pre-Prod. This normally involves a check to ensure all changes have been pushed to the candidate branch.
*  When testing is completed, the commit is promoted in Jenkins for the production release. 

*Release process*

The release process into production id currently handled by the WebOps team and requires a requests for change for each release. There is currently no DevOps or Continuous Delivery process in place either automated or manual.

*Test and production environments*

Four main environments, Development, Test and Pre-Production all managed by the development team. The Production environment.

* Jenkins pipeline - using docker containers an execution environment for the pipeline. We can build an environment on any promoted commit. 
* Jenkins automated tests - Test tests can be built and executed against any of the environments using the docker contains to execute. Each environment has its own set of tests with unique configuration
* Jenkins performance tests - Command line tests which can be executed through Jenkins. Remote server that host Jmeter and tests can be started in Jenkins.

*Automated acceptance tests*

The EA Queue Receiver Service is used as an orchestrator service to pick messages up from AWS SQS queues and send them to service API endpoints. Service API endpoint access through [Amazon API Gateway|https://aws.amazon.com/api-gateway/] is supported. The service is built on top of [PM2|https://github.com/Unitech/pm2], [sqs-queue-parallel|https://github.com/bigluck/sqs-queue-parallel] and [Amazon SQS|https://aws.amazon.com/sqs/] with *concurrency and parallel* message poll support.

The idea behind the Queue Receiver service is for the service to act as an orchestrator with any number of configured queues. Each queue has a dedicated queue receiver which continually polls the queue for new messages. Upon receipt of a message, the queue receiver will call aservice API endpoint to process it. If the message is processed successfully it will be deleted from the queue.

If message processing fails or the service API endpoint fails to respond, the message will be transferred to an error queue. Messages are held on error queues for a configurable amount of time before being transferred to another queue (usually the original queue).

*PM2* is used to control which queues are running and available programmatically.

description:
Planning applicants may need to carry out a flood risk assessment for proposed developments such as new building or an extension to an existing one. Members of the public or flood risk specialists can use the Flood Map for Planning (FMFP) system to find out which flood zone a proposed building site is in.

Users enter a location (postcode, national grid reference or easting and northing) and are presented with a map of their area of interest. One they have confirmed their location, they will be given information about their probability of flooding. If their location is in a flood zone, the user is informed that they need to carry out a flood risk assessment. They are also advised to check the Environment Agency’s standing advice. Links are provided to supporting information.

Users can also download the information as a PDF. The document includes the Environment Agency’s advice for the location of interest and a scaled map of the area. This document is called a Product 1 report.

In 2020, improvements to the Flood Map for Planning service are currently underway. They will include changes to the user journey and the inclusion of a Product 4 report. The product 4 report gives more detailed information about the flood risk of a development and is submitted as part of a flood risk assessment.

*Technologies:* Node.js, Hapi framework, PostgreSQL, Geoserver, OpenLayers, Amazon Web Services, Ordnance Survey Places API, Ordnance Survey Maps On Demand.

*URL:* [https://flood-map-for-planning.service.gov.uk/|https://flood-map-for-planning.service.gov.uk/]

*Source Code:* [https://github.com/DEFRA/fmp-app|https://github.com/DEFRA/fmp-app|smart-link] , [https://github.com/DEFRA/fmp-service|https://github.com/DEFRA/fmp-service|smart-link] , [https://github.com/DEFRA/fmp-tests|https://github.com/DEFRA/fmp-tests|smart-link]
